analysis.tldr: When global crude oil prices shoot up, imported fuel becomes costlier for India, threatening to push up domestic inflation and weigh on the rupee.
the_story: Indian government bonds fell in price as global crude oil prices surged past $90 and even topped $95 per barrel.
The Reserve Bank of India [India's central bank that controls interest rates and money supply] highlighted rising food inflation pressures, pointing to widespread price increases.
Higher oil prices threaten to widen the current account deficit [the gap between the money a country spends abroad versus what it earns] and negatively impact the rupee.
Investors are anticipating the monetary policy decision scheduled for December 4, with rate hikes expected.
analysis.what_happened: Indian government bonds dropped in value because global crude oil prices surged past $90 and $95 per barrel. This jump in oil costs sparked fears of rising inflation and economic instability, while the Reserve Bank of India also warned about persistent food price pressures.
analysis.analogy: It is like running a household vehicle where petrol suddenly becomes much more expensive, leaving you with less money to save or spend on other essentials.
why_it_matters_india: Global crude oil prices climb above $95 per barrel -> India has to spend significantly more dollars to import its oil.
Higher import costs widen the trade deficit and put pressure on the currency -> The rupee weakens (each rupee buys fewer dollars).
Pricier oil and stubborn food inflation push overall costs higher -> The Reserve Bank of India faces pressure to keep interest rates high or raise them further.
Higher interest rate expectations cause bond prices to tumble -> Borrowing costs for the government and eventually everyday loans get more expensive.

impacts.rationale: Costlier oil imports mean India needs more dollars, which weakens the local currency and makes imported goods pricier for everyone.

impacts.target: 10-year bond yield (interest India pays to borrow)
impacts.rationale: As bond prices tumble due to inflation fears, yields (the actual returns/interest rates) rise, which is bad because it pushes up overall borrowing costs.
Surging global crude oil makes raw fuel more expensive to buy and refine, hurting household budgets at the pump.
Combined pressures from expensive oil and rising food prices mean everyday goods and services cost more for ordinary consumers.

watch_next: The upcoming Reserve Bank of India monetary policy decision on December 4
Further movements in global crude oil prices
Domestic food inflation data
analysis.caveats: If global crude oil prices suddenly reverse and drop back down, these domestic inflation and currency pressures could ease quickly.

events.article_text:
Libya Plans New Oil Bidding Rounds Despite Mounting Security Risks

What I Cover Irina Slav has been writing about global energy markets since 2007, covering the oil and gas industry, energy security, commodities, and the…

Crude oil prices bounced back in early Asian trade on Thursday, climbing higher after fresh reports of tankers hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz and the latest Yemeni Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia, which targeted a refinery.

At the time of writing, Brent crude was trading at $95.30 per barrel, with West Texas Intermediate at $84.36 per barrel. The rise follows several days of losses as traders focused on predictions of a supply overhang, ignoring the mine strike reports. However, the frequency of these reports, coupled with data showing the average daily flow of energy commodities out of Hormuz, seems to have broken through the glut wall, pushing prices higher.

Iranian state media reports of tankers hitting mines in Hormuz have become a daily occurrence recently, with some days seeing more than one incident, prompting tanker tracking firms such as Kpler to report a decline in daily average flows of crude out of the Persian Gulf. These reports are undermining the glut story, showing that exports of crude from the region are still—or once again—significantly lower than they were before the United States and Israel first attacked Iran at the end of February.

The Houthi attack on Ras Tanura, the largest refinery in Saudi Arabia, contributed to the change in trader perception, a reminder that there is a war in the Middle East and the prospect of peace remains quite remote. The Ras Tanura refinery is located on Saudi Arabia’s eastern coast, on the Persian Gulf, and is part of a major oil export hub.

“The broadening of the Middle East conflict threatens to halt the recovery in oil flows in recent weeks. Persian Gulf crude exports rose last week but remain on a declining trend,” ANZ analyst Daniel Hynes said, as cited by Reuters.

Energy analyst John Kemp, meanwhile, noted that global oil stocks had gone up in October but “the increase has been underpinned by a shuttle run and naval blockade of Iran organised by the United States that is very costly to enforce and may be unsustainable both financially and operationally in the medium term.”

analysis.tldr: Rising global crude oil prices due to Middle East conflicts will make petrol, diesel, and everyday goods costlier in India, while putting pressure on the rupee.
the_story: Crude oil prices bounced back in early Asian trade on Thursday, with Brent crude trading at $95.30 per barrel and West Texas Intermediate at $84.36 per barrel.
The price jump was driven by fresh reports of oil tankers hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz and a Yemeni Houthi drone attack targeting the Ras Tanura refinery in Saudi Arabia.
Tanker tracking firms like Kpler reported a decline in the daily average flow of crude oil out of the Persian Gulf due to these incidents.
Traders previously ignored these risks expecting a supply glut, but the frequent attacks and lower export volumes forced them to push prices higher.
analysis.what_happened: Global oil prices rose sharply because ongoing attacks on oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and a refinery strike in Saudi Arabia disrupted oil shipments from the Middle East. Traders panicked about potential shortages, overcoming earlier predictions of a global oil surplus.
analysis.analogy: It is like a major highway carrying vegetables into a city suddenly getting blocked by hazards; even if there are vegetables piled up in the fields, fewer trucks are getting through, so prices in the city skyrocket.
why_it_matters_india: India imports a vast majority of its crude oil needs from global markets.
Higher international crude prices force oil companies to pay more dollars to buy oil.
India has to spend more of its foreign exchange reserves to buy dollars, which causes the rupee to weaken.
Costlier oil feeds into higher transport, manufacturing, and consumer goods inflation across the country.

impacts.target: Crude oil import costs for India
impacts.rationale: Global benchmarks like Brent crude rising to $95.30 per barrel directly make buying imported oil more expensive for India, which is generally bad for the economy.
India needs more US dollars to pay for costlier oil, increasing demand for dollars and weakening the rupee, which makes all imported goods pricier.
Higher fuel and transport costs drive up the prices of everyday goods and services, which is bad for household budgets.
Global geopolitical tensions and conflict in the Middle East drive investors toward safe-haven assets like gold, pushing domestic prices higher.

watch_next: Daily reports on oil tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz
Updates on the status of oil production facilities and refineries in Saudi Arabia
analysis.caveats: If military tensions ease quickly or tanker traffic normalizes, oil prices could reverse course and fall back down.

events.article_text:
On Wednesday, the USTR unveiled tariff proposals targeting 14 economic jurisdictions with two distinct rates, a higher one proposed as part of the Sec 301 probe, and a lower deal rate if the countries agree to a trade pact with the US

Indian exporters on Thursday urged the government to seal a trade pact with the US at the earliest, saying the proposed 17 per cent tariff, as outlined in the USTR report, would give India an advantage over competing nations.

They said that this is the right time to finalise the deal as exporters are getting good orders from the US buyers.

"India should do the trade deal as soon as possible. We are getting a lot of orders from the US, and further opening of the market will help increase exports," Federation of Indian Export Organisations (FIEO) President S C Ralhan said.

He added that the absence of a trade deal with the US could hurt India's exports by putting domestic exporters at a disadvantage compared with competitors from countries that enjoy lower tariff rates.

This could affect the price competitiveness of Indian goods in the US market, making it difficult for exporters to retain existing buyers and secure new orders, Ralhan said.

He added that the agreement should be balanced and reciprocal, safeguard India's long-term economic and developmental interests, and ensure that Indian exporters can compete on a level playing field with suppliers from other countries in the US market.

"While the industry is concerned with these developments as it raises uncertainty, there is no panic amongst exporters," he said.

Ralhan also called for clarity on how the proposed measures would interact with existing duties under Sections 301 and 232 and how the product-specific exemptions in the USTR notice would apply.

"Clear rules on the duties payable on each product would help exporters quote prices with confidence and avoid overlapping tariff burdens," he said.

FIEO urged negotiators to secure competitive tariff treatment for Indian products, address non-tariff barriers and improve market access.

It called for particular attention to MSMEs, which have less room to absorb sudden increases in duties and compliance costs.

The Federation also urged close consultations between the government and industry to assess the impact on each sector and prepare submissions for the USTR's public consultation process.

Sharing similar views, Ramesh Kumar Juneja, Chairman, Council for Leather Exports (CLE), said that the proposed 17 per cent tariff will be the "best deal" for India.

"We would urge for early finalisation of the deal. The proposed tariffs on India is lower than its competitors," Juneja said, adding that India is in a better position than Bangladesh and Vietnam.

Rafeeq Ahmed, chairman of leading leather and footwear products, Farida group, too said that the deal is "very" important for India.

"The key takeaway from the USTR report is that the proposed tariff on Indian goods is lower than that on Vietnamese goods. This will make Indian products more competitive in the US market," he said.

The US on Wednesday proposed 25 per cent tariffs on imports from India, with a provision to cap them at 17 per cent if the two countries agree to a bilateral trade deal, giving it a slight edge over Asian competitors.

The proposed tariffs followed investigations by the US Trade Representative into 16 economic jurisdictions -- China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan, Norway, Mexico and India -- relating to structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors.

Under the proposed USTR tariffs, Indian imports face a 17 per cent tariff if a trade pact is finalised, offering a calculated one per cent edge over Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Thailand (18 per cent deal rate) and a three per cent edge over Vietnam and China (20 per cent deal rate).

India, in its negotiations with the US on the trade deal, has been insisting on a competitive advantage over its Asian rivals, a demand that Washington has addressed in the tariff proposals. However, it was not immediately clear whether the one percentage point differential addresses the concerns flagged by India.

The EU, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Switzerland face 15 per cent tariff rates, inclusive of standard import duties. Vietnam would face tariffs of 20 per cent if the trade deal is finalised.

The USTR has decided to schedule public hearings on its proposals on January 25 and sought written comments from interested persons by January 5 as part of the final regulatory requirements before the tariffs come into effect.

The investigation began last March, after the Supreme Court overturned the indiscriminate trade levies imposed by the Donald Trump administration invoking the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA).

After that reversal, the USTR opened two investigations based on Article 301: one directed at 60 jurisdictions (about a hundred countries) for violating export regulations on forced labour; and the other against 16 jurisdictions for promoting surplus production.

India and the US are negotiating an interim bilateral trade agreement after the framework they finalised in February went back to the discussion board, with the Supreme Court striking down the IEEPA tariffs imposed last year.

India is seeking lower tariffs for its goods in the US market than its competitors such as Bangladesh, Vietnam and Cambodia.

analysis.tldr: A proposed US trade deal could make Indian goods cheaper to import than those from Vietnam and Bangladesh, potentially bringing more export orders to Indian factories.
the_story: On Wednesday, the United States Trade Representative (USTR) proposed a 25 per cent tariff [tax on imported goods] on Indian imports, which can be capped at 17 per cent if India and the US sign a bilateral trade deal.

Indian export bodies like the Federation of Indian Export Organisations (FIEO) and the Council for Leather Exports urged the government to seal the pact quickly because the proposed 17 per cent deal rate is lower than what rival nations face.

Under the proposal, India would get a one per cent edge over Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Thailand (at an 18 per cent deal rate) and a three per cent edge over Vietnam and China (at 20 per cent).
The USTR scheduled public hearings for January 25 and invited written comments by January 5 before finalizing the rules.
analysis.what_happened: The US proposed new import taxes targeting 14 economic jurisdictions following investigations into manufacturing overproduction. For India, the US offered a lower tax rate of 17 per cent as an incentive to finalize a bilateral trade agreement, creating a relative price advantage over Asian competitors like Vietnam and Bangladesh.
analysis.analogy: It is like a shopkeeper getting a lower wholesale tax rate than neighboring shops, allowing them to price their goods slightly cheaper and win over more customers.
why_it_matters_india: The USTR proposes a 17 per cent tariff for India if a trade pact is signed, compared to higher rates for rivals like Vietnam (20 per cent).
Indian exporters expect this relative tariff advantage to help secure more orders from US buyers.
Higher export volumes can boost revenues for Indian manufacturing and export sectors, particularly labor-intensive ones like leather and footwear.
However, failing to sign the deal could leave Indian goods at a price disadvantage in the crucial US market.

impacts.target: Export revenues for Indian manufacturing and leather/footwear companies
impacts.rationale: Lower relative tariffs than regional competitors could increase orders from US buyers, which is generally good for domestic manufacturing growth.
Higher export earnings bring more foreign currency into India, which helps strengthen the rupee (making each rupee buy more dollars) — good for importers and travelers.

watch_next: The USTR public consultation process and written comments deadline on January 5
Progress on bilateral trade agreement negotiations between India and the US
analysis.caveats: The proposed tariff numbers are part of a draft regulatory process and could change depending on the outcome of public hearings and ongoing negotiations.

the_story: The article argues that time-limited and auctioned export quotas work better than blanket trade restrictions.

analysis.analogy: It is like a popular shopkeeper limiting how many items each customer can buy and selling those limited passes to the highest bidder, rather than locking the shop doors completely.
why_it_matters_india: Governments around the world sometimes restrict or quota what goods they sell to other nations.
If global trading partners change how they limit exports, it forces international buyers to look for new suppliers.
Indian manufacturing companies and exporters watch these global trade rule changes closely to find new customers.
Shifts in global trade rules eventually ripple into how much foreign money enters India and how much Indian businesses earn.

Global trade policy changes create mixed sentiment for major companies trading internationally, affecting overall stock market mood.

analysis.tldr: When the central bank buys fewer foreign dollars, it affects how much the rupee changes in value against global currencies.
the_story: The Reserve Bank of India (the RBI, India's central bank that manages money and interest rates) saw its net dollar purchases drop heavily to $6.9 billion in September.
This is a sharp fall from $43.2 billion in August.

The massive buying in August was driven by inflows under a special scheme called FCNR(B) (Foreign Currency Non-Resident Bank deposits, a special type of bank account for people living abroad to keep money in foreign currencies in India).
During September, the rupee depreciated 0.9% (the rupee weakened, meaning each rupee buys fewer foreign dollars).
India's real effective exchange rate (a measure of the rupee's value compared to a basket of foreign currencies, adjusted for inflation) improved to 93.14 in October.
analysis.what_happened: The RBI bought significantly fewer US dollars from the market in September compared to August. This happened because August had a massive one-time rush of money coming into special nonresident bank accounts. Without that giant wave of cash, the central bank's dollar purchases dropped back down, while the rupee weakened by 0.9% during the month.
analysis.analogy: It is like a corner shop owner who suddenly had a huge cash day because an uncle sent money from abroad, but the next month things went back to a normal, smaller daily total.
why_it_matters_india: The RBI buys or sells dollars in the market to manage the value of our currency.
When special foreign inflows slow down, the central bank buys fewer dollars.
This shift coincides with the rupee weakening against the dollar by 0.9% in September.
A weaker rupee makes imported goods like crude oil more expensive for India, which can eventually lead to higher everyday prices.

impacts.rationale: The rupee depreciated 0.9% in September as the extra foreign inflows dried up, which makes imports costlier for everyday consumers.
The rate improved to 93.14 in October, showing a shift in how our currency stands globally when adjusted for inflation.

watch_next: Future trends in foreign currency deposits coming into Indian banks
How much the RBI intervenes in the currency market next month
analysis.caveats: Global currency markets can change rapidly based on sudden shifts in US interest rates or foreign investor behavior.

events.headline: India’s kharif foodgrains estimate 5% lower on weather woes

items.title: India’s kharif foodgrains estimate 5% lower on weather woes
items.summary: Rice output pegged 2.3% lower as Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan said farmers had to face challenges of lower rainfall, gap in spells of rain and damages due to cyclone and floods

items.title: India’s kharif foodgrains estimate 5% lower on weather woes
items.summary: Rice output pegged 2.3% lower as Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan said farmers had to face challenges of lower rainfall, gap in spells of rain and damages due to cyclone and floods

events.article_text:
India’s kharif foodgrains output in the 2026-27 season has been estimated lower by 5.1 per cent at 167.14 million tonnes (mt) from 176.04 mt a year ago. Rice production is pegged 2.3 per cent lower at 121.91 mt from 124.76 mt.

Releasing the first advance estimates of crop output, Union Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan said that despite the challenges due to deficient monsoon, Indian farmers have produced higher than the last five years’ average.

Admitting that the current year’s production has been pegged lower due to lower acreage, less rainfall, wide gap between rain spell and damage from cyclones and floods, he said still the country has sufficient foodgrains in stocks and the marginal fall in rice production willnot have any impact.

Asked about high prices of pulses and oilseeds which have adversely affected consumers, he said: “Most of the crops are selling either at their minimum support prices (MSPs) or higher levels. Let farmers also get some good prices. The government is also taking care of interests of the consumers.”

The estimates also show that only urad (black gram), jowar (sorghum), sunflower and jute production has increased from the previous Kharif season, whereas all other crops output is lower.

The pulses production is estimated to drop 6.2 per cent to 7.13 mt from 7.6 mt. Tur (red gram) output is pegged 13.1 per cent lower at 3.12 mt from 3.59 mt and that of moong (green gram) 14 per cent lower at 1.66 mt from 1.93 mt. But, urad production is estimated to have increased 28.3 per cent to 1.45 mt from 1.13 mt.

Among oilseeds, whose total production is seen to fall 10.2 per cent to 23.95 mt from 26.67 mt, soyabean output has been pegged 18.7 per cent lower at 10.24 per cent from 12.6 per cent while groundnut is seen to drop 1.5 per cent to 11.17 mt from 11.34 mt. Sunflower output has been estimated at 117,000 tonnes this year against 88,000 tonnes in 2025-26 Kharif.

Jowar production has been seen to be higher by 13 per cent at 1.48 mt from 1.31 mt, whereas bajra (millet) is likely to drop 5.7 per cent to 8.94 mt from 9.48 mt and ragi 37.5 per cent to 1.25 mt from 2 mt. On the other hand, maize production has been significantly impacted as the first estimate pegs it 14.6 per cent lower at 26.06 mt against 30.51 mt year-ago.

Total coarse- and nutri cereals’ production may fall 12.8 per cent to 38.11 mt this season from 43.68 mt year-ago, the agriculture ministry said in a statement.

Among cash crops, sugarcane production is likely to have dropped 9.1 per cent to 454.34 mt from 500 mt and cotton by 14.3 per cent to 24.87 million bales (of 170 kg each bale) from 29.02 mb. However, jute and mesta production is seen to grow 3.3 per cent to 9.71 million bales (of 180 kg each bale) from 9.4 mb.

analysis.tldr: Lower food crop production due to bad weather could keep prices for pulses, oilseeds, and sugar high, meaning higher grocery bills for your household.
the_story: India's kharif (monsoon-sown) foodgrains output for the 2026-27 season is estimated 5.1 per cent lower at 167.14 million tonnes, down from 176.04 million tonnes last year.
Union Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan stated the drop was caused by lower acreage (planting area), less rainfall, gaps between rain spells, and damage from cyclones and floods.
Rice production is pegged 2.3 per cent lower at 121.91 million tonnes, though the government says the country has sufficient stocks and the fall is marginal.
Pulses production is estimated to drop 6.2 per cent (with tur down 13.1 per cent and moong down 14 per cent), and total oilseeds production is seen falling 10.2 per cent.
Cash crops also took a hit, with sugarcane dropping 9.1 per cent and cotton falling 14.3 per cent.
analysis.what_happened: India's government released its first advance crop production estimates for the 2026-27 season, showing a 5 per cent drop in overall foodgrains. This decline was caused by weather woes including deficient rainfall, long dry spells, and damage from cyclones and floods during the monsoon season.
analysis.analogy: It is like a farmer's vegetable garden producing fewer vegetables because of a bad storm and dry spells, meaning there is less food to sell and prices at the local market go up.
why_it_matters_india: Bad weather leads to lower crop harvests across rice, pulses, oilseeds, and sugarcane.
Lower supply in the market pushes up the prices of key items like pulses (dal) and cooking oils.
Higher food prices increase overall inflation (the rate at which prices rise), making daily household shopping costlier.
The government maintains sufficient foodgrain stocks, which helps prevent extreme rice shortages.

impacts.rationale: Fewer crops mean pricier food items like pulses and cooking oils, which pushes up inflation and is bad for household budgets.
Lower production for pulses and oilseeds means tighter supply, leading to higher costs at the grocery store for everyday consumers.
Higher raw material costs for agricultural inputs can squeeze company profits, which may indirectly affect stock valuations for investors.

watch_next: Subsequent advance estimates from the agriculture ministry
Retail prices of pulses and cooking oils in local markets
Government steps regarding imports or stock releases to control food prices
analysis.caveats: These are only the first advance estimates, and final production numbers could change depending on subsequent weather conditions and winter crop harvests.

events.headline: How Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia impacts China’s AI supply chain

items.title: How Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia impacts China’s AI supply chain
items.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang attends a summit at the Institute of Peace on October 8, 2026 in Washington, DC.

events.article_text:
Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday, days after he admitted to having an affair with a Chinese data center executive, whom the U.S. intelligence agency believed to be a Chinese government agent. On Wednesday, The New York Times reported that Huang also had an affair with an Nvidia executive.

Nvidia’s board said that chief financial officer Colette Kress will serve as the company’s interim chief executive until a permanent successor has been named.

Huang’s exit has triggered worries about Nvidia’s future as the world’s top chipmaker, and about the entire AI industry where Nvidia has been a hardware provider, an investor, and a community leader. Repercussions from the saga will impact China, which has yet to replace Nvidia chips with domestic alternatives, as well as Taiwan and South Korea, which host a vast network of Nvidia suppliers.

Here are the key questions emerging from Huang’s dramatic downfall.

Jensen Huang had been the biggest advocate for selling chips to China, which he argued helps America maintain its market dominance.

Despite the U.S. banning the export of advanced Nvidia chips to China, Chinese companies have been trying to access chips remotely by working with data centers in Southeast Asia.

Alice Huang, with whom Jensen Huang had an affair, served as the executive of Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, one of Nvidia’s biggest customers in Southeast Asia. The Information reported that Alice Huang helped move about 240,000 H100, H200 and some A100 chips into China. Her companies also invested in DeepSeek, promising to supply Nvidia chips.

The Nvidia scandal will likely lead the U.S. government to tighten chip controls. Anticipating a crackdown, Chinese AI labs are trying to lock in overseas supplies of Nvidia chips, while traders in China are stockpiling restricted chips, Reuters reported.

Chinese chips are catching up in performance, but Nvidia chips are still essential to the AI industry.

In the first half of the year, Nvidia shipped 678,000 AI accelerators in China, down 44% from a year earlier and making up 34% of the market, according to a Reuters report, citing IDC data. In the same period, leading Chinese chipmaker HuaweiiHuaweiHuawei is a Chinese technology company focused on mobile phones and telecommunications, and is seen as a poster child for China’s global tech ambitions.READ MORE shipped 572,000 ‌AI ⁠accelerators, up from more than 300,000 a year earlier, accounting for 28% of the market,

AlibabaiAlibabaAlibaba, founded in 1999 by Chinese entrepreneur Jack Ma, is one of the most prominent global e-commerce companies that operates platforms like AliExpress, Taobao, and Tmall.READ MORE’s chip unit T-Head had 7% of the market, followed by Cambricon’s 5%. BaiduiBaiduBaidu is a Chinese technology company that operates the country’s biggest search engine and video-streaming service iQiyi.READ MORE subsidiary Kunlunxin held 4% and Hygon had 3%.

Although AI labs are increasingly working with chipmakers to make sure their models can run on domestic infrastructure, most AI developers still train new models on Nvidia chips. Nvidia’s B300 delivers 6.75 times the arithmetic performance of Huawei’s best Ascend 950 chip, according to research firm Epoch AI. Huawei also lags behind Nvidia in production volume.

Jensen Huang enjoys rock star status across Asia, especially in his birth country Taiwan, where he would visit night markets, share snacks with fans, and host banquets with executives of Taiwanese suppliers. He said the company planned to invest $150 billion a year in Taiwan.

Many internet users expressed disappointment that they lost a role model in tech. Some wrote that the spy allegations and the criticisms of Huang would add to the discrimination of Asians working in America’s tech industry.

Huang’s departure is also creating uncertainty around Nvidia’s supply chain relationship with Asian companies. But several executives at Nvidia’s Taiwanese suppliers said they still expected steady orders from Nvidia in the coming years because of the sustained demand from the AI industry, according to Taiwan’s Central News Agency.

MinoHealth researchers in Ghana jailbroke their own LLM as a test. What emerged were thousands of toxin recipes—and an urgent push for regulation.

Ending U.S. visa sponsorship and shifting roles abroad helps the company retain talent, but leaves employees paying a steep financial and personal price.

In her new book “Reboot: AI and the Race to Save Democracy,” writer Beth Simone Noveck warns that while AI can increase efficiency, predictive models pose significant ethical and societal risks.

analysis.tldr: The sudden departure of Nvidia's boss could trigger stricter US rules on selling advanced computer chips, which may ripple through global technology markets and ripple into Indian tech outsourcing services.
the_story: Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday following an affair with a Chinese data center executive linked by US intelligence to the Chinese government, and another affair with an Nvidia executive.
Chief financial officer Colette Kress will serve as interim chief executive while a permanent successor is chosen.
Alice Huang, the data center executive in Singapore, reportedly helped move about 240,000 advanced Nvidia chips into China and invested in DeepSeek.

In the first half of the year, Nvidia shipped 678,000 AI accelerators (specialized computer chips designed to train artificial intelligence) in China, down 44% from a year earlier, while Chinese rival Huawei shipped 572,000.
Nvidia's B300 chip delivers 6.75 times the arithmetic performance of Huawei's best Ascend 950 chip, and Nvidia's Taiwanese suppliers still expect steady orders due to high global demand.
analysis.what_happened: Nvidia's top boss Jensen Huang resigned abruptly after admitting to an affair with a Chinese executive whom US intelligence suspected of being a government agent. This scandal has sparked fears of tighter US export restrictions on advanced technology, pushing Chinese labs and traders to quickly stockpile chips while shaking up the leadership of the world's most vital AI hardware provider.
analysis.analogy: It is like the captain and star salesman of the world's biggest engine factory suddenly being forced to step down due to a scandal, making everyone wonder if the factory will still be allowed to ship engines across borders.
why_it_matters_india: US-China tech tensions tighten further due to the scandal surrounding Nvidia's former boss.
Global tech companies face higher regulatory risks and uncertainty over chip supplies.
Indian IT (Information Technology) services and tech consulting firms relying on global AI software development experience shifting project pipelines.
Investor sentiment swings across global technology stocks, affecting Indian stock market indices that track global tech trends.

impacts.rationale: Sudden leadership changes and potential regulatory crackdowns typically create panic among investors, which is generally bad for short-term market stability.

impacts.target: Indian tech stocks like TCS & Infosys
impacts.rationale: Global tech hardware disruptions can delay major artificial intelligence and software projects for Western clients, affecting Indian IT earnings — generally bad for stock investors.
Global technology jitters can cause foreign investors to pull money out of emerging markets like India, which can push local index prices down.

watch_next: Announcements from the US government regarding tighter export controls on advanced computer chips
Updates from Nvidia's interim chief executive Colette Kress on future supply chain plans
analysis.caveats: If Nvidia's board names a permanent replacement quickly and reassures suppliers, market jitters over the chip supply chain could fade faster than expected.

events.headline: Australia’s conflict prevention choice: build the system, not just the parts

items.title: Australia’s conflict prevention choice: build the system, not just the parts
items.summary: A new parliamentary report’s conflict tools only work together, backed by early warning that tracks resilience as well as risk.

events.article_text:
Australian and Solomon Islands joint maritime surveillance from a RAAF C-27J Spartan, 13 August 2026 (Clarke-Kelly/Department of Defence)

A new parliamentary report’s conflict tools only work together, backed by early warning that tracks resilience as well as risk.

The most-pressing world events explained by Lowy Institute experts and global contributors, in your inbox, every Thursday.

Australia’s conflict prevention choice: build the system, not just the parts

Foreign Minister Penny Wong told parliament this week that Australia must be “as committed to preventing wars as we are to ending them” (Opens in new window), including by “addressing the drivers of conflict before tensions become crises”. Whether that commitment is pursued seriously, across all tools of statecraft, will depend on putting a system in place (Opens in new window) to deliver it.

Today, parliament’s Joint Standing Committee on Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade tabled its report (Opens in new window) on the inquiry into the role of Australia’s international development program in preventing conflict. Its recommendations are a chance to put the system in place that the Foreign Minister’s commitment depends on.

The tensions that tore through Solomon Islands in the early 2000s had been building for years: land disputes, youth unemployment, distrust of weak institutions. Australia’s response, the Regional Assistance Mission to Solomon Islands (RAMSI), cost $2.6 billion (Opens in new window) in its first decade. No one can say if the violence could have been prevented, but the warning signs were visible years earlier.

A resilience lens adds a different question: what is holding societies together, and is it getting stronger or weaker?

Conflict prevention is now an established Australian foreign policy priority. The push has centred on deterrence and diplomacy to manage the biggest geostrategic risks. The role of development cooperation in helping prevent conflict is less clear, as is the relationship of all three tools in an explicit Australian approach (Opens in new window).

The inquiry set out to address this. The first ten recommendations in its report ask the Government to keep doing what works to prevent conflict: steady development funding, support for gender equality and Women, Peace and Security, inclusive development, strong public institutions, and conflict sensitivity. The report also backs something the humanitarian sector has long sought: a standing sanctions exemption for legitimate humanitarian assistance.

Most interestingly, the report sets out the parts of a conflict prevention system: an explicit conflict prevention statement covering conflict within and between states, a central function and a thematic ambassador in DFAT, conflict sensitivity training and resources, conflict prevention indicators and reporting, and stronger early warning that triggers coordinated action. Coalition members’ additional comments (Opens in new window) argue that overall aid levels fall outside the inquiry’s remit, but do not dissent from these recommendations.

The key question for the government’s response to the inquiry is whether it takes up these recommendations as a system or cherry-picks from them.

The risk is a response that picks the easiest recommendations and notes the rest. But a conflict prevention statement will stay on paper unless a central team and an ambassador in DFAT drive it. They will do little more than share information unless early warning shows them where risk is building. And without indicators to track progress and report on it, no one will know whether the statement is being delivered.

Early warning is what lets the other parts act in time. To do that well, it needs to be built to track resilience as well as risk.

Early warning that monitors only risk often sounds the alarm once protesters are already on the streets and the prevention window has narrowed. A resilience lens adds a different question: what is holding societies together, and is it getting stronger or weaker? Tracking resilience over time alongside risk would give Australia a clearer picture of where tension is building while there is still time to act. DFAT told the inquiry (Opens in new window) it could strengthen its use of early warning and resilience monitoring.

It is also a quick win. It could be piloted with modest funding in a few countries where Australia has deep relationships. Coalition members stress that aid effectiveness depends on “how funding is targeted and used”. Targeting it well needs a shared view of where resilience is shifting and risks are building.

That picture has to cover the full range of conflict risk. The OECD’s latest fragility assessment (Opens in new window) rates six contexts in Southeast Asia and the Pacific as highly or extremely fragile. In the Pacific, local grievances and geostrategic competition feed each other (Opens in new window). The committee rightly asks for the conflict prevention statement and DFAT’s central function to cover conflict within states as well as between them. Early warning needs to watch both, or it will miss half the picture.

In Southeast Asia, the Iran war has pushed up fuel and food prices and is straining budgets. Yet in the Development Intelligence Lab’s latest Pulse Check (Opens in new window), nearly 100 experts across nine countries still named climate change the decade’s most defining disruption, as did respondents to ISEAS’s most recent survey (Opens in new window). The inquiry report calls climate change a threat multiplier of conflict risk. The Southeast Asia Pulse Check experts’ top priority for partners was national resilience systems that can manage compounding shocks. So, a prevention system built around resilience would start from what partners themselves are asking for.

RAMSI in Solomon Islands showed what reacting late costs Australia and its neighbours. The Foreign Minister has made prevention a priority, and parliament has set out what

analysis.tldr: Geopolitical stability in Australia's region and global commodity shifts mean Indian markets and import costs face minimal direct shocks from this report, keeping domestic fuel and food prices steady for now.
the_story: Australia's parliamentary Joint Standing Committee on Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade tabled a report on using international development programs to prevent conflict.
Foreign Minister Penny Wong stated that Australia must be as committed to preventing wars as ending them by addressing drivers of conflict early.

The report recommends setting up a conflict prevention system, including a central team and thematic ambassador in DFAT (Australia's Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade), clear indicators, and a standing humanitarian sanctions exemption.
The article notes that an earlier intervention in Solomon Islands (RAMSI) cost $2.6 billion in its first decade after warning signs were missed.
Separately, the text mentions that the Iran war has pushed up fuel and food prices and strained budgets in Southeast Asia, while climate change is viewed as a major threat multiplier.
analysis.what_happened: An Australian parliamentary committee released a report arguing that Australia needs a connected system of tools—such as early warning systems, development aid, and diplomacy—to prevent foreign conflicts before they erupt, rather than just reacting late. The report responds to growing global instability and past expensive interventions like the one in Solomon Islands.
analysis.analogy: It is like servicing your car regularly to stop the engine from blowing up on the highway, instead of just paying for expensive towing and repairs after it breaks down.
why_it_matters_india: Australia releases a report on foreign aid and conflict prevention -> Australia adjusts its diplomatic and aid spending in the Indo-Pacific region.
The Iran war strains Southeast Asian budgets and lifts fuel and food costs -> Global energy and commodity markets experience price volatility.
Global commodity price pressures ripple through import bills -> India's imported inflation and domestic consumer price index see indirect pressure.
International trade routes and regional stability remain key for supply chains -> Indian manufacturing and exports maintain steady shipping corridors.

impacts.rationale: Ongoing conflicts mentioned in the region continue to strain energy supplies, which can make fuel costlier for everyday Indian consumers.
Higher global food and fuel prices from regional wars can increase everyday household expenses in India, which is generally bad for consumers.
Global supply shocks and higher energy import bills can weaken the rupee slightly, making imported goods more expensive.

watch_next: How the Australian government responds to the parliamentary committee's recommendations
Developments in the Iran war and its ongoing impact on global fuel and food prices
analysis.caveats: The article text cuts off near the end, and the report's recommendations are focused on Australian internal policy rather than direct global financial interventions.

events.headline: IREF say non-basmati rice export bans are unlikely, but urges exporters to remain cautious

items.title: IREF say non-basmati rice export bans are unlikely, but urges exporters to remain cautious

events.article_text:
Updated - November 26, 2026 02:55 pm IST - COIMBATORE:

India’s substantial rice stocks provide an important cushion for domestic supply. File. | Photo Credit: Reuters

The government is unlikely to impose restrictions on non-basmati rice exports over the next month, the Indian Rice Exporters’ Federation (IREF) said on its portal on Wednesday (November 26, 2026).

It, however, urged rice exporters to continue business with appropriate contractual and inventory safeguards.

The Federation claimed that based on information received from sources familiar with policy discussions, its current assessment was that while policy options remain under consideration, there is no indication of an immediate move to curb exports.

However, the possibility of export duties or other policy measures cannot be ruled out, particularly if domestic rice prices continue to rise.

However, strong international demand continues to influence domestic market dynamics. Any further significant icrease in domestic prices can prompt a review of the export policy.

the_story: On November 26, 2026, the Indian Rice Exporters’ Federation (IREF) stated that the government is unlikely to restrict non-basmati rice exports over the next month.
Despite this reassurance, IREF urged exporters to use proper contracts and keep safety stock as precautions.
The assessment is based on insider information about policy discussions, though export duties or other measures remain a possibility if domestic rice prices keep rising due to strong global demand.
analysis.what_happened: The Indian Rice Exporters' Federation (IREF) announced that immediate bans on non-basmati rice exports are not expected. This assessment comes from sources close to policy discussions who note that India's current rice stockpiles are safely protecting local supplies.
analysis.analogy: It is like a grocery shop owner who has plenty of dal in the back room, so they are allowed to sell to customers outside for now—but they must keep an eye on local prices so they do not run short.
why_it_matters_india: IREF says export bans are unlikely for the next month -> Indian rice exporters can continue fulfilling overseas orders without sudden government blocks -> Strong international demand keeps pulling local rice toward global buyers -> If domestic rice prices keep climbing due to this high demand, the government may step in with export duties (taxes on goods sent abroad) or new curbs -> Lower risk of sudden export bans keeps business predictable for now, but rising local prices remain a threat to household food budgets.

impacts.target: India's inflation rate (rate at which everyday prices rise)
impacts.rationale: If strong global demand keeps pulling rice out of the country and domestic prices keep rising, food staples become costlier for everyday families — generally bad for consumers.

impacts.target: Rice export businesses & agricultural trading stocks
impacts.rationale: Knowing that export bans are unlikely for the next month lets companies safely plan shipments and revenue, which is good for their business continuity.

watch_next: Movement of domestic rice prices in local markets
Any official government announcements regarding export duties
analysis.caveats: The outlook could change rapidly if domestic rice prices accelerate faster than expected, prompting the government to override these expectations and impose sudden restrictions.

history.title: The crisis that taught Asia to hoard dollars
history.what: Thailand ran out of reserves defending its currency peg and let the baht float. It fell 50% in months. The panic spread through Indonesia, South Korea and Malaysia within weeks, becoming the worst emerging market crisis of the era.
history.why: These economies had borrowed heavily in dollars while earning in local currency — a mismatch that is invisible while the exchange rate is fixed and fatal the moment it moves. Their central banks had promised stable pegs, which encouraged still more dollar borrowing. When growth slowed and the dollar strengthened, speculators tested the pegs and the reserves ran out.
history.impact: Indonesia's economy shrank 13% in a year and its government fell. South Korea, a developed economy, needed the largest IMF bailout in history to that point. Millions fell back into poverty. Asian shares lost 60-80% in dollar terms.
history.policy: IMF bailouts with severe conditions, which remain bitterly resented in the region. More durably, the affected countries abandoned rigid pegs, let their currencies float, and began accumulating enormous foreign exchange reserves as self-insurance so they would never have to ask again.
history.consequence: Asia's reserve hoard is the direct descendant of 1997. Those reserves were recycled into US government bonds, which helped hold global interest rates down for two decades — one of the quiet forces behind the cheap money of the 2000s, and therefore behind the housing bubble that followed.
history.pattern: Borrowing in a currency you do not earn is the most reliable way to turn a slowdown into a collapse. It is invisible in good times and decisive in bad ones. Check what currency a country, a company or a project owes in.
history.india_echo: India was barely touched, because the capital account was still largely closed and the rupee was not freely convertible. The lesson Indian policymakers drew — open up slowly, keep reserves large — still shapes RBI policy today, and explains why India has weathered every emerging market scare since with discomfort rather than disaster.
history.watch_for: Countries with large dollar debts, thin reserves and a currency the central bank insists is stable. The combination is the setup, every time.
